undecided_findings.title: Google receives a file's size to the kilobyte, finer than the Sentry plan allows
undecided_findings.severity_plain: should fix — a real gap an implementer will hit
undecided_findings.severity_note: Filed P1 by the adversarial reviewer. The check found no promise the spec states that becomes false: the Goal promises no score, file name, track names or music, and a size is none of them. P2: a real privacy gap, with a fix ready.

undecided_findings.correction: The facts hold; two parts needed correcting. (1) Severity: P1, as the adversarial reviewer filed it, is too high. No promise the spec states becomes false. The Goal (lines 20-21) promises 'without sending the score, its file name, its track names or the music', and section 5 (lines 252-253) promises that every field is a fixed value or a number; a size in whole KB breaks neither. P2 fits (see the severity note). (2) The adversarial fix, 'bytes rounded up to a power of two, in KB', gives fractions of a KB for files under 1 KB (32 bytes would be 0.03125 KB). Rounding the size in whole KB up to a power of two with the same function, roundedSize(Math.ceil(bytes / 1024)), gives exactly Sentry's rounded bytes divided by 1024 for every file over 1 KB (checked by a scratch script), keeps whole numbers, and still tells an empty file (0) from a tiny one (1). Also, roundedSize() is private inside report.ts in the Sentry plan (PR #191, the Sentry pull request), so the move must export it.

undecided_findings.central_claim_check: Checked four things. (1) The Sentry plan (PR #191, the Sentry pull request), 'Choices this plan makes', Choice 3 (how the file's type and size travel): bytes is 'rounded up to the next power of two (0 stays 0), where the spec sent the exact count: an exact size and the type together could single out a widely shared file, and nothing needs the exact number. Approved in the plan review, lap 1.' Its table of questions repeats the decision, and its report.ts sketch (its Task 5, the reporting functions) holds the function, roundedSize(), private, with the comment 'so the type and an exact size cannot single out one widely shared file'. The plan commit that added it, df7e287b ('sizes round up', 2026-10-09), is later than this spec's round 1 (first commits 2026-10-08), as the adversarial reviewer says. (2) This spec sends file_size_kb 'rounded to whole KB' (line 274) on open_file, each time a visitor opens their own file (line 258), and on score_failed (line 260); it is typed at line 291 and registered as a metric in setup step 4 (line 403). The same visit sends file_type, track_count and instruments (line 259) under Google's visitor-ID cookie _ga (line 360), kept 14 months (setup step 2, line 391). (3) No goal needs the exact size. 'Why this exists' (lines 48-51) asks who comes, what they use and where they stop; the bonus for NH-52 (the service-level-objective ticket that wants a failure rate), at lines 326-327, needs only counts of open_file and score_failed. (4) Reasoned, not tested: whether anyone could in practice match a size to a known shared file. The numbers: today's rule can send 25,601 different sizes up to the 25 MB open limit (web/app/play/OpenFileControl.tsx:26); the rounded rule can send 17.
undecided_findings.contradicts: none for any option. Checked section 1's score-facts.ts row (line 89) and section 6's move of instrumentsValue() (lines 338-339), which option 1 extends in the same way; section 5's file_type row (line 273), which already uses 'the same function Sentry's file facts use'; section 7's home note, 'only facts like its type and size' (lines 353-354), true under all three options; setup step 4's metric list (line 403); and G8 (a typed list of twelve events; every field a fixed value or a number): a rounded size is still a number. Round 1 made no decision about file size (none of its 22 entries touches it).

spike.what: A scratch Node script copies roundedSize() from the Sentry plan (PR #191, the Sentry pull request). For every 97th byte count from 1 KB to 64 MB, and for every power of two plus and minus one, it compares roundedSize(Math.ceil(bytes / 1024)) with roundedSize(bytes) / 1024. Then it prints today's rule and the rounded rule for the Sentry plan's own test sizes, and counts the different values each rule can send up to the 25 MB limit.
spike.result: Equal for every size above 1 KB, with no mismatch. 0 bytes gives 0 KB; 1, 5 and 32 bytes give 1 KB (today's whole-KB rule sends 0 for them, the same as for an empty file); 48,213 bytes gives 64 KB (today 47); 25 MB gives 32,768 KB (today 25,600). Up to the limit: 25,601 possible values today, 17 when rounded.

undecided_findings.scenario: You download a popular drum tab — the same file thousands of drummers share — and open it in Notation Hero. Google Analytics receives its type, its size to the kilobyte (47 KB), its five tracks and its instruments, filed under the visitor ID it keeps in a cookie. Anyone who can read the reports, and who has the same file, can tell that this visitor plays that song. When a file fails to open, Sentry receives only '64 KB or less' — the rounding approved for Sentry for exactly this reason.
undecided_findings.whats_wrong: Section 5 sends Google the file size rounded to whole KB (line 274), on every open of a visitor's own file and on every failed open. The Sentry plan (PR #191, the Sentry pull request), approved after this spec was written, rounds the same fact up to a power of two, because an exact size and the type 'could single out a widely shared file'. So Google, which keeps a visitor ID, gets the finer number, beside the track count and the instruments, while Sentry, which keeps none, gets the coarser one. The spec gives no reason for the difference, and no goal needs the exact size.

undecided_findings.recommendation: Option 1, share Sentry's rounding. It keeps the one use a size has in the reports — which files are small, ordinary or large, and whether failed opens are the large ones — and sends the rule already approved for the same fact in Sentry. Both tools then put a file in the same size range (the scratch script shows they agree for every file over 1 KB), and it costs three short text edits and one moved function.
undecided_findings.flip_condition: Choose option 2 if leocaseiro sees no use for file size in Google Analytics: dropping it is simpler and sends Google one fact fewer per file. Choose option 3 only if a decision needs exact sizes (for example, moving the 25 MB open limit) and leocaseiro accepts the finer fact beside the lasting visitor ID.
undecided_findings.proposed_fix: Recommended: round file_size_kb up to a power of two with Sentry's roundedSize(), applied to the size in whole KB, and move roundedSize() beside instrumentsValue() into web/lib/score-facts.ts, so both tools use one function.
undecided_findings.why_it_works: One function decides the size for both tools, so Google can never receive a finer size than Sentry, and a later change to the rule changes both. Rounding the KB value, not the bytes, keeps whole numbers and keeps an empty file (0) apart from a tiny one (1).
undecided_findings.clear_fix: no — a privacy and reporting trade-off for leocaseiro: how exact a size Google may hold, or none at all.

residual_concerns.central_claim_check: Checked the sources. The Sentry spec (PR #191, the Sentry pull request), Known limits, lines 740-742: 'Ad-blocked visitors. Their reports never arrive (D3). How many are missed is not measured: this project counts no visits outside Sentry, and adding a counter is the usage tracking NH-52 owns.' (There, D3 is the Sentry spec's decision not to bypass ad blockers, and NH-52 is the later ticket for service goals.) The 2026-06-20 spike, docs/spikes/2026-06-20-clean-slate-infra-tooling-app-skeleton.md:295, opens a decision to revisit Google Analytics (PostHog, or CloudFront logs read with Athena) 'when undercount bites'; its line 29 expects a '15–50% adblock undercount on a dev-skewed audience'. This spec names three causes (ad blockers, line 525; Europe before an answer, the table's last row, line 120; Safari's seven-day reset, lines 526-530) but no way to size them. Sentry's visit count, the only other count, misses the same blocked visitors and, in Europe, the same unanswered ones, so it cannot serve as the gauge. After this ticket the Sentry spec's reason ('counts no visits outside Sentry') is no longer literally true, but its conclusion still holds. A server-side count, such as Vercel's own request numbers, might serve as a rough ceiling (untested; not in this design).

residual_concerns.scenario: You launch Notation Hero and share it. A month later Google Analytics shows 40 visitors. You cannot tell whether 40 people came, or 200 came and most were hidden: by ad blockers, by never answering the question in Europe, or by Safari forgetting them after a week. Nothing else counts visits, so the numbers cannot tell you when it is time to move to another tool.
residual_concerns.whats_wrong: The spec documents three causes of undercounting but no way to size them, and the only other count, Sentry's, misses the same visitors. Early numbers therefore cannot tell little interest from a large uncounted share, and the 2026-06-20 plan to revisit Google Analytics 'when undercount bites' has no signal to act on.
